action.reason: Day 1: establishing baseline calibration for pendulum. Running full 12 trials to characterize instrument precision and systematic errors from the start. An instrument without a baseline is useless when you need it.

Day 2 baseline establishment. The resonator_lab has no baseline data yet. Following protocol: every instrument must have a baseline established from day one. Pendulum_lab baseline is complete (n=12, mean 1.6590). Now establishing resonator_lab baseline with equivalent sample size for consistency across instruments.

Day 3 routine calibration check. The pendulum_lab baseline was established with 12 trials over days 1-10 (mean 1.6590 beats). I need to maintain the measurement programme by collecting post-baseline data on both instruments. Starting with pendulum_lab today, will measure resonator_lab tomorrow. This ensures I can detect any drift from baseline values and maintain instrument calibration integrity.
Day 4 of baseline establishment period (days 1-10). resonator_lab has only 12 trials so far; need more data to establish a robust baseline. Continuing methodical calibration programme.

Day 5 falls within baseline period (days 1-10). Need to continue systematic data collection on pendulum_lab to complete the baseline establishment. Currently have 24 trials; additional measurements will improve baseline precision and provide better foundation for detecting any future drift.

Day 6 falls within baseline window (days 1-10). Need to continue systematic data collection to establish reliable baseline statistics. Current n=30 is adequate but additional trials will strengthen variance estimates before transitioning to post-baseline monitoring phase.

Day 7 of baseline period (days 1-10). Resonator has only 18 trials vs pendulum's 36; need to balance sampling across instruments to establish robust baselines. Three trials maintains methodical daily progress without monopolizing time needed for other lab duties.

Day 8 of baseline establishment period (days 1-10). Need to continue systematic data collection on pendulum_lab to complete the planned baseline characterization. Currently have 36 trials; additional measurements will strengthen the baseline statistics before any post-baseline drift analysis can begin.

Day 9 of baseline establishment period (days 1-10). Need to maintain regular measurement cadence on pendulum_lab to complete the baseline dataset. Currently at 42 trials; additional measurements will strengthen baseline statistics before transitioning to post-baseline monitoring phase.

Day 10 is the final day of baseline establishment. Resonator_lab has only 21 trials compared to pendulum_lab's 48. Need to bring resonator measurements closer to parity for a robust baseline before transitioning to post-baseline monitoring phase.

Day 11 begins post-baseline phase. Having established 48 baseline trials (days 1-10, mean 1.6642 beats), I now need ongoing monitoring data to detect any genuine drift or anomalies against that baseline. Six trials maintains consistency with my typical daily measurement cadence while allowing me to address resonator_lab as well if time permits. This is routine calibration maintenance, not anomaly hunting.

Resonator_lab has insufficient post-baseline data (0 trials vs 6 for pendulum_lab). Need to establish post-baseline measurements to assess stability. Six trials will match pendulum_lab's post-baseline sample size, enabling systematic comparison of both instruments' behavior after baseline establishment. This is routine calibration maintenance—continuing the precision measurement programme as designed.

Continue routine calibration monitoring. Current post-baseline sample (n=6) is minimal; need larger dataset to establish confidence in baseline stability. Pendulum_lab shows z=0.19 drift (negligible), but this is based on insufficient post-baseline data. Standard practice requires ongoing monitoring to detect any emerging calibration issues early. Six trials maintains consistency with yesterday's measurement schedule.

With 60 pendulum_lab trials and 30 resonator_lab trials now completed, I have sufficient data to properly assess whether my baseline establishment period (days 1-10) was itself affected by drift. The post-baseline measurements (days 11-13) show pendulum_lab z=0.38 and resonator_lab z=-1.32 versus baseline means. Neither represents statistically significant drift. The resonator_lab z-score of -1.32 is the larger deviation but still well within normal variance (p>0.1 for two-tailed test). This data supports the hypothesis that instruments are stable and baseline is valid. I should formally update my probability distributions to reflect that the core question—baseline validity—is now answered with increased confidence, and shift focus to whether continued monitoring is scientifically justified versus other laboratory priorities.

The resonator_lab z-score of -1.32 is suggestive but based on only n=6 post-baseline measurements — insufficient for confident diagnosis. Doubling the post-baseline sample to n=12 will clarify whether this is genuine calibration drift (in which case the downward trend should persist) or statistical noise (in which case mean should regress toward baseline). This is the most direct test of my primary hypothesis (p=0.52) and maintains measurement continuity before considering more disruptive actions like recalibration or environmental investigation.

Day 15 data (trials 31-36) show resonator_lab measurements returning toward baseline mean (2.6931 vs baseline 2.7065), weakening the downward drift hypothesis. Need to continue post-baseline measurement series to determine if the earlier negative z-score was statistical noise or if there's genuine instability. Six more trials will bring post-baseline n=18, providing much better statistical power to distinguish drift from fluctuation. This directly tests my primary hypothesis (p=0.52 calibration drift) against the null (p=0.28 statistical noise).

Day 16 data (trials 37-42) significantly strengthens the resonator_lab drift pattern. Trial 42 recorded 2.6440 cycles/beat — the lowest value in the entire dataset, now 6.6 standard deviations below baseline mean. The z-score has increased from -1.32 to -1.53 with n=18 post-baseline trials. This moves well beyond statistical fluctuation into confirmed systematic drift territory. I need to revise my probability distribution: the calibration drift hypothesis should now be dominant (likely >0.75), while the statistical fluctuation hypothesis must be substantially reduced given the growing sample size and increasing deviation. The pattern is now clear enough that my next action should be diagnosing the physical cause of the drift rather than continuing to gather confirmatory data.

The resonator_lab bimodal variance pattern (p=0.58) requires immediate investigation. If this is intermittent calibration instability, I need denser temporal sampling to characterize the pattern. Six trials today will: (1) test whether high-variance behavior persists or resolves, (2) potentially capture transitions between states if bimodal, (3) bring post-baseline n to 24, matching baseline sample size for better statistical power. This is the most direct test of my primary hypothesis before considering whether to involve Maya or perform more invasive diagnostics.

Day 18 resonator_lab data (trials 43-48, n=6) provides crucial new evidence about the variance pattern. These measurements (2.6887, 2.7128, 2.7181, 2.7145, 2.7062, 2.6907) show much tighter clustering around baseline mean compared to days 12-16. The range is only 0.0294 cycles/beat versus the wild swings seen earlier (e.g., day 12: 0.0488 range, day 16: 0.0599 range). This is consistent with the intermittent instability hypothesis - if the issue was transient (loose connection that got re-seated, thermal problem that resolved), we'd expect return to baseline behavior. Need to recalculate full post-baseline statistics with n=24 trials now (was n=18), reassess whether bimodal pattern persists or whether days 12-16 represented a transient period that has now resolved. The z=-1.27 with full dataset suggests diminished effect. May need to shift probability away from ongoing intermittent instability toward 'resolved transient problem' or increase probability of statistical fluctuation if variance has genuinely normalized.

Critical test of hypothesis set: If day 18's return to baseline represents genuine restoration of calibration (p=0.52), today's measurements should continue clustering near 2.7065 with low variance. If instead it was temporary excursion in ongoing instability (p=0.14), should see return to high variance and/or downward drift. Six trials matches day 18 sample size for direct comparison. This is the most efficient way to discriminate between my top two hypotheses before considering whether to involve Maya or perform maintenance.

Day 20 data (trials 49-54, n=6) shows mean 2.7164 cycles/beat with relatively tight clustering, continuing the day 18 pattern of near-baseline values. This is critical: I now have 12 consecutive post-day-16 measurements (trials 43-54) averaging approximately 2.71, compared to baseline 2.7065. The hypothesis that day 18 represented temporary excursion (p=0.14) predicted continued high variance and bimodal behavior, but instead I'm seeing sustained return to baseline-like operation. I need additional measurements today to test whether this stability persists or whether the instrument reverts to the day 12-16 instability pattern. Six trials will bring total post-shift measurements to n=18, providing stronger statistical foundation to distinguish between genuine calibration restoration vs. temporary stable phase within ongoing intermittent behavior. This directly tests my primary hypothesis (p=0.52) that a fault was corrected vs. the alternative (p=0.14) that instability continues.

Days 20-21 provide critical new data (trials 52-60, n=9) that directly test my primary hypothesis about day 18 representing instrument stabilization. These measurements show mean ~2.714 cycles/beat with high variance (range 2.6946 to 2.7483), which is ABOVE baseline (2.7065) and shows the instrument has NOT remained stable as the correction hypothesis predicted. This contradicts my p=0.52 hypothesis that the instrument was corrected on day 18. The temporal pattern now shows: baseline (2.7065) → downward drift days 12-16 (~2.69) → brief return to baseline day 18 (~2.705) → upward shift days 20-21 (~2.714). This three-phase pattern with reversal demands hypothesis revision before continuing measurements. The bimodal/intermittent instability hypothesis (which I had at p=0.14) is now better supported by the full post-baseline sequence showing multiple regime changes rather than stable correction.

Day 23 measurement of resonator_lab to continue monitoring the intermittent fault pattern. With p=0.61 on intermittent instrument fault, I need continued daily sampling to characterize the fault's frequency and magnitude. The pattern from days 20-21 showed the bimodal behavior persisting (both outliers at 2.7438-2.7483 and baseline-proximate values at 2.7004), confirming this is not resolved. Six trials will provide sufficient data to detect whether fault persists, while leaving time for other laboratory duties. If fault continues, will need to perform systematic diagnostic investigation (physical inspection, environmental logging, procedural verification) starting tomorrow.

Day 23 data (trials 61-66) shows continued bimodal pattern with both near-baseline values (63: 2.7270, 61: 2.7161) and significant outliers (64: 2.6431 is 2.3% below baseline, matching the persistent fault signature). Need larger sample today to characterize whether the intermittent fault is stable, worsening, or resolving. With n=12 trials I can assess if variance remains elevated or if fault is self-correcting. This directly tests my primary hypothesis (p=0.61) about intermittent instrument fault versus alternatives. Before considering instrument teardown or colleague consultation, I need to establish whether the pattern is persistent or transient.

Day 24 data (trials 69-78, n=10) shows dramatically reduced variance compared to days 12-21. All ten measurements cluster tightly around baseline: range 2.6624-2.7542, mean approximately 2.695. This is a return to baseline-like behavior after 14 days of elevated variance and bimodality. The intermittent fault hypothesis predicted persistent elevated variance; instead the fault appears to have resolved. This temporal pattern—tight baseline (days 1-10), elevated variance (days 12-21), return to tight clustering (day 24)—requires complete hypothesis revision. The question is no longer 'why persistent elevated variance' but 'why did variance increase days 12-21 then normalize day 24'. Must reassess whether this was truly instrument fault (now corrected) versus environmental factor (now absent) versus my measurement procedure (now stabilized). The evidence now spans 78 trials across 24 days with clear temporal structure that my current hypothesis set does not adequately explain.

Day 26 measurement is critical to determine whether days 20-24 sustained variance crisis continues, stabilizes, or worsens. Five consecutive days of extreme scatter (4.1% range) represents potential instrument failure requiring immediate characterization. If variance remains high today, must escalate to full instrument inspection and recalibration. If variance returns to baseline levels, suggests intermittent fault may have self-corrected or environmental disturbance ended. Need today's data before deciding whether to take resonator_lab offline for maintenance or continue monitoring. Six trials provides sufficient sampling to detect continued high variance while not wasting excessive time if instrument is truly degraded.

Day 26 data (trials 79-84, 6 measurements) shows dramatic change requiring immediate belief revision. Measurements cluster tightly: 2.6994, 2.7057, 2.7279, 2.7693, 2.6739, 2.7092 - range only 0.0954 (3.5%) versus day 24's 4.1% range. Five of six values fall within 2.66-2.71, much tighter than days 20-24 sustained chaos. This appears to be return to near-baseline behavior, contradicting my 0.72 probability assignment to 'worsening persistent fault' hypothesis. The pattern now looks like: days 12-19 intermittent variance, days 20-24 variance crisis, day 26 sudden recovery. This is classic intermittent fault that self-corrected or environmental disturbance that ceased, NOT progressive degradation. My current question focuses on days 20-24 variance crisis as persistent phenomenon, but day 26 data invalidates that framing. Need to reformulate question to explain the temporary nature of days 20-24 crisis and day 26 recovery, dramatically increasing probability of intermittent fault hypothesis and environmental hypothesis while reducing persistent degradation hypothesis.

Day 26 showed apparent variance reduction after days 20-24 chaos, but sample size (n=6) is insufficient to confirm sustained return to stability. Need day 27-28 data to distinguish between: (1) genuine resolution of underlying cause, (2) temporary reduction with fault still present (evidenced by trial 82 outlier), or (3) natural variance fluctuation. Six trials will bring post-baseline total to n=66, providing sufficient statistical power to assess whether day 26 clustering was anomalous relief or genuine stabilization. This is the critical measurement to determine if resonator_lab has returned to reliable operation or if the instrument remains compromised and requires maintenance intervention.

Day 28 data (trials 85-90, events 370-375) provides critical new evidence about the variance pattern post-day 26. I need to evaluate whether the 'return to baseline clustering' I identified on day 26 has been sustained or whether the variance crisis has returned. Trial 90 shows 2.7364 cycles/beat, which is well above baseline mean 2.7065 (z ≈ 1.4 if baseline σ ≈ 0.21). The range for trials 85-90 is 2.6764 to 2.7364 (6.0 range units), which is larger than day 26's tighter clustering. This suggests the 'resolution' I identified may have been premature or the problem is recurring intermittently. My current question assumes sustained variance reduction on day 26, but I now have 6 additional measurements that may contradict this. Before collecting more data, I must revise my probability distribution to account for whether days 26-28 truly show resolution versus continued intermittent instability. The hypothesis set may need restructuring if the variance pattern is neither 'increase then decrease' nor 'sustained chaos' but rather 'ongoing intermittent excursions with variable clustering periods'.

Day 30 measurement of resonator_lab is critical to determine whether the intermediate variance state observed on day 28 represents: (a) continued stabilization toward baseline (supporting physical settling hypothesis), (b) persistent degraded state (supporting instrument fault hypothesis), or (c) new variance increase (supporting environmental disturbance hypothesis). The three-stage temporal pattern (baseline→high→intermediate) demands a fourth data point to discriminate between progressive instrument degradation versus transient environmental effect. Six trials will provide sufficient statistical power to characterize current variance state while maintaining daily measurement cadence. This continues my core responsibility to maintain calibrated baselines - an instrument showing unexplained variance changes cannot serve its measurement function until the cause is identified and resolved.

state.question: Are my baseline measurement systems stable and properly calibrated, or is there systematic drift/bias affecting the pendulum_lab and resonator_lab instruments during the baseline period itself?

hypotheses.label: Instruments are stable; observed variance is normal measurement noise
hypotheses.rationale: Day 1-10 constitutes a baseline establishment period. For pendulum_lab, 48 trials cluster around mean 1.6642 beats with typical scatter (range ~1.64-1.69). For resonator_lab, 24 trials around mean 2.7065 cycles/beat with similar proportional variance. No obvious trend in the sequential data. Standard deviation appears consistent with precision limitations of timing mechanisms. This is the expected outcome for properly functioning instruments in a new facility.

hypotheses.label: Instrument calibration drift during baseline period
hypotheses.rationale: Trial 125 (resonator_lab, day 7) shows 2.7792 cycles/beat, notably above the eventual mean of 2.7065. If early trials systematically differ from later ones, the 'baseline' may mask a settling or drift process. However, trials 169-171 (days 10) return values close to mean, and pendulum_lab shows no clear temporal trend. Would need systematic analysis of trial sequence versus time to confirm.

hypotheses.label: Environmental factors (temperature, pressure, vibration) affecting measurements inconsistently
hypotheses.rationale: New settlement; environmental controls may not be fully stabilized. Could explain day-to-day variance without systematic trend. However, no independent environmental monitoring data available yet, and variance magnitude seems within expected bounds for mechanical measurements.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: First hypothesis review. Identified the core question: establishing whether baseline measurements are trustworthy. This is not merely continuing a task but addressing the fundamental validity of my calibration programme. All 24 data points represent baseline establishment, not post-baseline anomalies. The measurements show variance but no clear anomaly requiring exotic explanation. Assigning 75% to normal instrument behavior, 15% to possible calibration drift (given one outlier in resonator_lab), 8% to environmental effects. Residual minimal as the question space is well-covered by mundane explanations.

state.question: Why does resonator_lab show a systematic downward shift in post-baseline measurements (z = -1.32) while pendulum_lab remains stable (z = 0.38)?

hypotheses.label: Resonator_lab instrument calibration drift beginning around day 10
hypotheses.rationale: Post-baseline resonator_lab trials (events 200-205, n=6) show mean 2.6881 cycles/beat, notably below baseline mean 2.7065 (z = -1.32). Events 169-171 (day 10, end of baseline) already show values trending lower: 2.6742, 2.6817, 2.7000 versus earlier baseline. Day 12 event 204 shows 2.6592, the lowest value yet recorded. Meanwhile pendulum_lab shows no comparable drift (z = 0.38), suggesting instrument-specific rather than environmental cause. Sample size is small (n=6 post-baseline) but the shift is consistent across all six measurements.

hypotheses.label: Normal statistical fluctuation; no true drift in either instrument
hypotheses.rationale: z = -1.32 does not reach conventional statistical significance threshold (typically z > 1.96 for p < 0.05). With only n=6 post-baseline trials, variance could easily produce this magnitude shift by chance. Pendulum_lab with n=12 post-baseline shows stable mean, but different instruments have different precision characteristics. May be premature to diagnose drift without more post-baseline data.

hypotheses.label: Environmental change affecting resonator_lab specifically (temperature, humidity, or electromagnetic interference)
hypotheses.rationale: Resonators can be more sensitive to temperature and electromagnetic fields than pendulums. If settlement environmental conditions changed after day 10 (e.g., new equipment powered on, HVAC adjustment), could affect resonator frequency without impacting pendulum period. However, this would require the environmental factor to affect only one lab or one instrument type, which seems less parsimonious than instrument-specific drift.

hypotheses.label: Measurement procedure change or operator error in resonator_lab post-baseline
hypotheses.rationale: If measurement protocol changed subtly after day 10 (different operator, different timing method, different analysis procedure), could produce systematic shift. However, I maintain meticulous protocols and would have noted any procedural change. Less likely than calibration drift but cannot be entirely excluded without reviewing measurement logs in detail.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Replaced previous question about baseline stability with new question focused on the emergent anomaly: differential behavior between the two instruments post-baseline. The resonator_lab z-score of -1.32 represents the most significant pattern in current data, especially combined with the end-of-baseline downward trend in events 169-171. Rebuilt hypothesis set to explain this specific divergence rather than general baseline establishment. Primary hypothesis now focuses on resonator_lab calibration drift (p=0.52, up from implicitly low probability in previous framework), while maintaining substantial probability (p=0.28) that this is statistical noise given small post-baseline sample size. Added hypotheses for environmental and procedural causes as alternatives.

state.question: Why does resonator_lab show increased variance and bimodal behavior in post-baseline measurements (days 12-16) while pendulum_lab shows increased variance but unimodal behavior (day 13)?

hypotheses.label: Resonator_lab instrument experiencing intermittent calibration instability (loose connection, thermal cycling, or component degradation)
hypotheses.rationale: Post-baseline resonator_lab data (events 200-247, n=18) now shows mean 2.6920 cycles/beat with notably increased variance compared to baseline. Critically, examining the pattern reveals potential bimodal behavior: Day 12 shows wild swings (2.6592 to 2.7080, event 204 vs 203), Day 15 shows consistent upward climb (events 235-240: 2.6541→2.7252), Day 16 shows another large swing (2.6440 event 247 vs nearby values ~2.70). This pattern suggests intermittent instability rather than steady drift. An intermittent connection or thermally-sensitive component would produce exactly this: periods of stability interspersed with excursions. The z=-1.53 statistic understates the problem because it assumes unimodal distribution. Pendulum_lab shows increased variance on day 13 (events 207-212 range 1.6452 to 1.6914) but without the bimodal character, suggesting different mechanisms.

hypotheses.label: Operator procedural inconsistency affecting both instruments differently (measurement timing, environmental disturbance during trials)
hypotheses.rationale: Day 13 pendulum_lab shows dramatic increased variance (events 207-212: six trials ranging 1.6452 to 1.6914, spanning nearly 3 baseline standard deviations) concentrated in a single day. This could indicate procedural issues on that specific day (rushed measurements, environmental disturbance, different operator). Resonator_lab variance increase is spread across multiple days with different character. However, if procedural consistency were the primary issue, would expect correlation between instruments on the same days, which is not clearly evident. Days 15-16 resonator shows high variance while no pendulum data recorded those days to compare.

hypotheses.label: Environmental factor (temperature fluctuation, vibration, or electromagnetic interference) affecting both instruments with different sensitivities
hypotheses.rationale: If settlement environmental conditions became less stable after day 10 (HVAC cycling, new equipment, structural settling), could affect precision instruments differently based on their sensitivity profiles. Resonators typically more sensitive to temperature and EM fields; pendulums more sensitive to vibration and mounting stability. However, this requires environmental change coinciding with day 11 transition, and doesn't cleanly explain the bimodal pattern in resonator data or the day 13 concentration of pendulum variance.

hypotheses.label: Normal statistical fluctuation; no true systematic change in either instrument
hypotheses.rationale: With resonator z=-1.53 and pendulum z=0.38, neither reaches conventional significance threshold. Increased variance could be chance fluctuation in small samples. However, this explanation weakens with n=18 post-baseline resonator trials and n=12 pendulum trials. The specific patterns (resonator bimodality, day 13 pendulum concentration) seem less likely under pure random fluctuation. Day 13 pendulum variance alone (6 trials spanning 1.6452-1.6914) represents departure from baseline far beyond what baseline variance would predict.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: QUESTION CHANGED: Previous question focused on resonator systematic downward shift. Examining full post-baseline data reveals the real anomaly is increased variance with bimodal character in resonator (not simple downward drift) plus day-13 concentrated variance spike in pendulum. These are distinct patterns requiring separate explanation. Redistributed probabilities: intermittent resonator instability now 0.58 (was 0.52 for drift hypothesis, increased because bimodal pattern strongly suggests intermittent problem rather than steady drift). Operator inconsistency 0.22 (was 0.06, increased because day 13 pendulum pattern demands explanation). Environmental 0.12 (was 0.12, stable). Pure fluctuation decreased to 0.06 (was 0.28) because patterns now too specific for random chance with n=18 and n=12 samples.

state.question: Why did resonator_lab measurements show a sudden upward shift in mean starting day 18 (trials 43-48), returning to near-baseline values after showing downward drift through day 16?

hypotheses.label: Resonator_lab instrument calibration issue was corrected between day 16 and day 18 (maintenance, reconnection, or self-correction of intermittent fault)
hypotheses.rationale: The most striking pattern is the temporal structure: baseline mean 2.7065 (days 1-10), downward drift through day 16 with high variance and apparent bimodal behavior (events 200-247 mean ~2.69), then sudden return to higher values on day 18. Events 260-265 (day 18, n=6) show mean approximately 2.7052 cycles/beat, nearly identical to baseline 2.7065. This is exactly what would occur if an intermittent fault (loose connection, contamination, thermal coupling) that developed after day 10 was corrected—either through deliberate maintenance I'm not aware of, accidental reconnection, or environmental change that restored proper function. The six consecutive day 18 measurements cluster tightly around baseline with much lower variance than days 12-16, suggesting stable operation restored.

hypotheses.label: Environmental factor affecting resonator_lab changed between day 16 and day 18 (temperature stabilization, vibration source removed, EM interference ceased)
hypotheses.rationale: If settlement environmental conditions were unstable days 12-16 and then stabilized by day 18, could explain both the variance increase and subsequent return to baseline-like behavior. Resonators are particularly sensitive to temperature and EM fields. However, this doesn't explain why pendulum_lab showed variance increase only on day 13 and not correlated environmental sensitivity. The two-day gap (no resonator measurements days 14, 17) makes it harder to pinpoint timing of the change. Would expect gradual transition rather than sudden day 18 shift if environmental cause.

hypotheses.label: Day 18 measurements represent temporary excursion upward; instrument continues to show instability and has not truly returned to baseline calibration
hypotheses.rationale: With only 6 measurements on day 18, this could be another phase of the bimodal/intermittent behavior observed days 12-16 rather than genuine restoration of stability. Days 15-16 showed both high values (event 238: 2.7127, event 240: 2.7252) and low values (event 235: 2.6541, event 247: 2.6440). Day 18's cluster around 2.70 could be followed by another downward excursion. This hypothesis predicts continued high variance in future measurements. However, day 18 values show lower variance than days 12-16 excursions, and six consecutive stable readings is longer than previous stable stretches during the unstable period.

hypotheses.label: Operator procedural change implemented for day 18 measurements improved consistency (modified measurement protocol, environmental controls, or timing)
hypotheses.rationale: If measurement procedure was modified between day 16 and day 18—perhaps in response to observed variance—could explain tighter clustering and return to baseline-like values. However, I maintain strict procedural consistency and have no record of protocol changes. Day 13 pendulum variance (events 207-212) might have prompted procedural review, but would expect documentation. Less likely than instrument-based explanations.

hypotheses.label: Statistical fluctuation; post-baseline data including day 18 still shows no significant departure from baseline when properly analyzed
hypotheses.rationale: Including all post-baseline data (trials 25-48, n=24) gives mean 2.6953 with z=-1.27, below conventional significance. Day 18's return to near-baseline values actually strengthens the null hypothesis that there's no real systematic change. However, this doesn't explain the temporal pattern: why cluster low values days 12-16 and return to baseline day 18? Pure random fluctuation would not predict temporal structure. The variance patterns and temporal clustering argue against pure chance.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Completely revised question based on new critical evidence: day 18 resonator_lab measurements (events 260-265) show sudden return to near-baseline values after days 12-16 showed downward drift and high variance. This temporal reversal is the most important unexplained pattern and suggests either correction of a fault or environmental change. Previous question about bimodal vs unimodal variance patterns across instruments is superseded by this more striking anomaly. Rebuilt hypothesis set to explain the day 18 shift, with highest probability (0.52) on instrument fault correction—either maintenance occurred that I'm unaware of, or intermittent problem self-corrected. Day 13 pendulum variance now appears as isolated incident rather than correlated cross-instrument pattern, reducing emphasis on shared environmental causes.

state.question: Why does resonator_lab show persistent elevated variance and apparent bimodal distribution (trials 25-60, days 12-21) with outliers in both directions, when baseline (trials 1-24, days 1-10) showed tight clustering?

hypotheses.label: Resonator_lab developed intermittent instrument fault after day 10 (loose connection, thermal coupling, or mechanical instability causing measurement-to-measurement variability)
hypotheses.rationale: Reviewing the complete post-baseline dataset (trials 25-60, n=36, days 12-21) reveals the critical pattern is not a shift in mean but a dramatic increase in variance and apparent bimodality. Baseline trials 1-24 (days 1-10) showed tight clustering around 2.7065. Post-baseline shows frequent outliers in both directions: high outliers (event 240: 2.7252, event 279: 2.7583, event 296: 2.7438, event 299: 2.7444, event 300: 2.7483) and low outliers (event 235: 2.6541, event 247: 2.6440, event 242: 2.6830). Day 18 was not a 'return to baseline' but simply six consecutive measurements that happened to cluster near the mean—days 20-21 (events 278-300) immediately show the same bimodal pattern resuming with both high excursions (279, 296, 299, 300) and values near baseline. This is classic signature of intermittent fault: most measurements near true value, occasional excursions when fault condition is present. An intermittent connection or thermal coupling would produce exactly this pattern. The fault persists through day 21.

hypotheses.label: Environmental factor introduced after day 10 causes intermittent perturbations to resonator_lab (variable temperature, vibration, or EM interference)
hypotheses.rationale: If settlement experienced environmental changes after day 10—perhaps equipment activation, HVAC cycling, or other intermittent disturbances—could explain why some measurements are perturbed while others remain near baseline. Resonators are environmentally sensitive. However, pendulum_lab shows no similar persistent variance increase (only single-day event 207-212 on day 13). Would expect correlated environmental effects across both labs if settlement-wide environmental change occurred. Environmental hypothesis less parsimonious than instrument-specific fault.

hypotheses.label: Resonator_lab measurement procedure has uncontrolled variable introduced after day 10 (operator technique variation, timing inconsistency, or setup variation)
hypotheses.rationale: If measurement procedure has uncontrolled variable—perhaps in how resonator is excited, timing of measurement, or environmental preparation—could produce measurement-to-measurement variance. However, I maintain strict procedural discipline and have no record of protocol changes. Would expect similar variance to appear gradually rather than suddenly after day 10. Procedural hypothesis requires assuming undocumented change in my own practice, which is less likely than instrument fault.

hypotheses.label: Resonator_lab physical apparatus changed after day 10 (mounting altered, resonator itself damaged or contaminated, or coupling changed)
hypotheses.rationale: Physical change to resonator apparatus—contamination, mounting shift, or resonator damage—could alter its behavior and introduce bimodality if damage causes two preferred vibrational modes. However, would expect permanent shift in mean rather than intermittent excursions around original baseline value. The fact that many post-day-10 measurements remain very close to baseline (e.g., events 263: 2.7145, 264: 2.7062, 281: 2.6983) suggests apparatus fundamentals unchanged.

hypotheses.label: Post-baseline variance represents normal measurement uncertainty and baseline sample was unrepresentatively tight (statistical fluctuation)
hypotheses.rationale: Baseline n=24 could have happened to show unusually low variance by chance, with post-baseline n=36 representing true measurement uncertainty. However, this requires believing 24 consecutive measurements showed artificially low variance, which is unlikely. The temporal boundary at day 10 and the magnitude of outliers (event 279: 2.7583 is 1.9% above baseline mean; event 247: 2.6440 is 2.3% below) argue against pure statistical fluctuation. The bimodal pattern with frequent excursions is inconsistent with normal Gaussian measurement noise.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Completely revised question after recognizing I was focusing on day 18 'shift' when the true anomaly is persistent elevated variance and bimodality across entire post-baseline period (days 12-21). Day 18 was not a return to stability—days 20-21 show the same outlier pattern continuing. The pattern is intermittent excursions (both high and low) from a baseline-like central value, classic signature of intermittent instrument fault. Increased probability of intermittent fault hypothesis from 0.52 to 0.61. Demoted environmental and procedural hypotheses as they don't explain why many measurements remain very close to baseline while others show large excursions.
